These ten hypotheses come from general knowledge of how NAS-Bench-201 cells behave. None of the 100 designed experiments have results yet, so none of the hypotheses has been tested.

1. **Removing edge 3 hurts more when edge 4 is none.** The 0→3 edge is then one of fewer routes into the output node.
2. **Removing edge 3 does better when it replaces avg_pool_3x3.** Dropping a parameter-free pooling shortcut costs little or may help, while dropping a conv loses capacity.
3. **Setting edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 5 was none.** That opens a new path from node 2 to the output instead of just swapping an op.
4. **Setting edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 5 was avg_pool_3x3.** Replacing pooling with a conv on an output edge is a large gain.
5. **Setting edge 3 to skip_connect helps more when edge 3 was none.** Adding a residual input-to-output shortcut is one of the strongest improvements in this space.
6. **Setting edge 3 to skip_connect helps less when edge 3 was nor_conv_3x3.** The shortcut then comes at the cost of a conv on the direct path.
7. **Setting edge 0 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 0 was none.** Node 1 then stops being dead, which revives edges 2 and 4.
8. **Setting edge 4 to avg_pool_3x3 does worse when it replaces nor_conv_3x3.** It trades a learnable conv for pooling on an output edge.
9. **Removing edge 1 hurts more when edge 0 is none.** Node 2 then loses its only live input, which kills edge 5's path to the output.
10. **Setting edge 3 to nor_conv_1x1 helps more when edge 3 was none.** It adds a new learnable direct path instead of replacing an existing op.
